beats.text: Syllabus four point one: use the principle that, when a particle is in equilibrium,
the vector sum of the forces acting is zero.
By the end you can check equilibrium in two directions.
Use two balances to find unknown forces.
And explain why balancing one direction is not enough.
We consider two perpendicular directions: horizontal and vertical.
Look at the sideways forces. Equal pulls to the left and right cancel each other.
The upward pull is larger, leaving a resultant upward. Sideways balance alone is not equilibrium.
Now make the upward and downward pulls equal. They cancel too.
The resultant is zero in each direction. That is equilibrium in two dimensions.
The vertical pair can be stronger than the horizontal pair. Compare opposite forces along the same direction.
Consider a small object being held in place by several pulls.
Two pulls act to the left, while one acts to the right.
Another pulls upward, and one pulls downward. Together they keep the object still.
We will use the sideways balance first, then the vertical balance, to find the unknown downward force. Here is the whole question.
The object is modelled as a particle in equilibrium. Find Q.
To the left act P newtons and twenty newtons.
To the right act thirty two newtons.
Upward act two P newtons, and downward act Q newtons.
The same P appears in two different forces. The upward force is twice the leftward P force.
All the arrows already represent forces in newtons. There is no mass to convert.
Which direction lets us find P first? Take a moment.
Horizontal has only one unknown, P. Vertically, both P and Q are unknown.
Take right as positive. Rightward force minus leftward force equals zero, because the particle is in equilibrium.
From the diagram, thirty two minus the total in brackets, P plus twenty, equals zero. Both leftward pulls belong inside those brackets.
Equivalently, P plus twenty equals thirty two. Total left equals total right.
Subtract twenty from both sides. P equals thirty two minus twenty.
P equals twelve. So the leftward force labelled P newtons is twelve newtons. Keep that value on the diagram.
Now look vertically. The sideways forces have no vertical effect. Only the upward and downward forces enter this equation.
Take up as positive. Upward force minus downward force equals zero.
Substitute the labels: two P minus Q equals zero.
So Q equals two P. The downward pull must match the upward pull.
We found P equals twelve. Therefore Q equals two times twelve.
Q equals twenty four. The unknown downward force is twenty four newtons.
Put it back on the diagram. Upward is also twenty four newtons. Leftward, twelve plus twenty balances thirty two to the right. Both directions balance.
Keep the horizontal forces unchanged. If only the downward pull becomes larger, is the particle still in equilibrium?
No. Horizontal balance survives, but the vertical resultant is downward. Both directions must balance.
You can now check equilibrium in two directions.
Use two balances to find unknown forces.
And explain why balancing one direction is not enough.
